content: In epidemiology, an epidemic is defined as the occurrence of new cases of a disease within a specific human population during a defined time period, at a rate that significantly exceeds what is expected based on recent historical data. The rate at which new cases appear in the population during this time frame is referred to as the incidence rate. When this phenomenon occurs in animal populations, it is termed an epizootic. The classification of an epidemic can be subjective, as it depends on what is considered expected or normal. An epidemic may be confined to a specific location, in which case it is referred to as an outbreak. It can also be more widespread, in which case it is called an epidemic, or it may even span the globe, in which case it is classified as a pandemic. Because the definition relies on what is deemed expected, even a small number of cases of a rare disease, such as rabies, may be classified as an epidemic, whereas a large number of cases of a common disease, such as the common cold, would not. Diseases that occur consistently at a relatively high rate within a population are referred to as endemic diseases. For example, malaria is considered endemic in certain regions of Africa, such as Liberia, where a significant portion of the population is expected to contract the disease at some point in their lives. The term epidemic is also used in a broader, non-infectious context to describe widespread and growing societal issues, such as obesity, mental illness, or drug addiction. Notable historical examples of epidemics include the bubonic plague epidemic in Medieval Europe, commonly known as the Black Death, and the Great Influenza Pandemic that coincided with the end of World War I. To mitigate the emergence of new epidemics, several preemptive measures have been proposed by experts such as Professor Nina Marano and Andy Dobson. These measures include reducing the consumption of animal protein (e.g., meat, milk, and dairy products), prioritizing the consumption of locally sourced food, eating crops that are in season, improving agricultural efficiency, avoiding the destruction of rainforests, and being willing to pay higher prices for meat. Additionally, other measures, such as implementing population control strategies and improving urban planning, are known to reduce factors that contribute to the emergence of new epidemics. These measures not only address the root causes but also decrease the likelihood of future epidemics. In August 2007, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported an unprecedented rate of propagation of infectious diseases, highlighting renewed global concern about the spread of such illnesses.
